source.title: Efficient Language Model Training through Cross-Lingual and Progressive Transfer Learning

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates zero-shot downstream scores for models of different sizes, which bears conceptually on V6. It does not fit or test the stated pretraining scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Hoffmann et al.'s compute-optimal token counts to contextualize its training runs, but does not test those laws. Its validation-PPL curves compare transfer methods at individual target model sizes; they do not fit a power law or test extrapolation. Downstream-score rows are included because the study reports zero-shot scores for differently sized models.
record.test_reason: This is a transfer-learning method paper (CLP-Transfer). It cites Hoffmann et al. only to explain why the BLOOM runs are under-trained, and fits no scaling law. The validation-PPL curves compare initialisation methods at fixed model sizes. Table 2's zero-shot scores benchmark the authors' models against other families. Those models differ in family, tokenizer, data, token count and initialisation, and the study analyses no relation between scale, or pretraining loss, and downstream performance. The authors' passing remark that only >6B models beat random is an aside, not a test of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. CLP-Transfer reaches the from-scratch PPL with 50% (GPT2) or 20% (BLOOM) of the tokens. Zero-shot German results are disappointing and mostly near random, and BLOOM-CLP 6.4B has the best average (0.43). The authors also attribute the poor zero-shot results to model size and token count being too small, and to poorly translated test sets.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains language models using cross-lingual and progressive transfer and evaluates transfer efficiency; it does not use the scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports differences by initialization/transfer method and model family; its downstream comparisons also vary in training data and token count.
record.problems: The study does not fit or test a scaling law. Downstream comparisons vary by model family, initialization, training data, and token count, so they do not isolate a scale or pretraining-loss relationship. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the downstream averages.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 also reports OSCAR validation PPL and six individual downstream-task metrics. These were left out because the rows retained record the table's reported aggregate downstream average for each model; the PPL and task-specific values are not separate tests of a fitted scale-to-performance relationship.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
No compute-optimal allocation test; Hoffmann et al.'s token counts are only cited.
No other modality or regime scaling. The transfer runs are not fitted to any law.
No analysis of downstream performance against scale or loss. Table 2 is a confounded cross-family benchmark.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels should be dropped. The comparisons mix model families, data, tokenizers and initialisation, and the study never treats them as a scale test. The XGLM sequence (0.32, 0.34, 0.40) is near the random baseline (0.38). The OPT embedding-similarity analysis across sizes (Fig. 1) concerns the method's assumption, not any version.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or test across parameters, tokens, or compute; the validation-PPL curves compare training methods rather than characterize a scaling law.
No small-run fit is extrapolated to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other-modality or alternative-regime scaling law is tested.
The study reports zero-shot task scores across models, but does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
No sensitivity analysis of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending.

relation.reason: Hoffmann et al. supply background and published token-budget reference points for interpreting under-training; the study neither fits nor tests a scaling law or uses one to implement CLP-Transfer.

tranche.reason: The experiments compare transfer initializations and downstream benchmarks; they do not test power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or predictable downstream scaling.

source_check.notes: All 13 averages and the random baseline match Table 2. These are method-benchmark results, not scaling-law evidence; the BLOOM transfer and from-scratch models also differ in architecture and training datasets (§4.3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: XGLM size comparison and BLOOM-CLP size comparison
reader_labels.reason: The reported average scores are higher for the larger model in each of these comparisons: XGLM 0.32, 0.34, 0.40 and BLOOM-CLP 0.26, 0.43 (R3–R5, R10–R11). These are score comparisons, not fitted predictions.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GPT2 model comparisons and overall cross-model evaluation
reader_labels.reason: The reported averages do not show a uniform relationship with size or training approach: the 117M GPT2-WECHSEL average is 0.35, while the 1.5B variants range from 0.24 to 0.34; the authors also describe most models as at or below the random baseline on average (R1, R6–R9, R12–R13).
